title: Chopsticks > Forks
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the history and culture of chopsticks. They cover their likely origins as cooking tools in China thousands of years ago (twigs for pulling food from boiling water), the role of population growth and cutting food into small pieces, the shift from millet gruel and spoons to wheat noodles, dumplings and sticky rice that made chopsticks the main eating utensil, and regional differences among China, Japan, Korea and Vietnam (Thailand largely doesn't use them). They discuss the silver-chopstick poison myth, chopstick shapes by country, the environmental toll of disposable chopsticks (Japan's wabashi, China's estimated eighty billion a year), and chopstick etiquette rooted in Japanese Buddhist funeral customs (no chopsticks upright in rice, no crossing them, no passing food chopstick to chopstick, no spearing or pointing). They also cover how to hold chopsticks, consecutive a phobia (fear of chopsticks), and a short listener mail segment about a Sammy Davis Jr. story.
topics: Stuff You Should Know listener mail

segments.title: Tour cancellation notice and opening banter
segments.summary: The hosts open with a message about postponed Portland and Vancouver shows due to the coronavirus, then banter about the movie Misery and the song Chopsticks.

segments.title: Origins and names of chopsticks
segments.summary: The hosts introduce chopsticks, note their age of thousands of years, and discuss the word origin and names in several languages. Early chopsticks were cooking tools used to pull food from boiling water, and later became eating utensils.

segments.title: Silver chopsticks, poison myth and joined chopsticks
segments.summary: They discuss the belief that silver chopsticks reveal poison, which doesn't work for cyanide but reacts to garlic or rotten eggs, and the Japanese origin of joined split chopsticks.

segments.title: Population, wheat, noodles and the rise of chopsticks
segments.summary: The hosts explain how population growth led to cutting food into small pieces, how wheat noodles and dumplings and then sticky rice replaced millet gruel and spoons, and why Korea kept the spoon alongside chopsticks.

segments.title: Regional chopstick shapes and disposable chopsticks
segments.summary: The hosts compare chopstick shapes in China, Japan and Korea and begin discussing the environmental problems of disposable chopsticks.

segments.title: Environmental impact of disposable chopsticks
segments.summary: They discuss the forests consumed by disposable chopsticks, with China's estimated eighty billion a year, Japan's preference for disposable wabashi since 1978, usage shares by country, and efforts such as a Chinese tax on disposables.

segments.title: Chopstick etiquette and taboos
segments.summary: The hosts go through chopstick etiquette, especially Japanese, including taboos tied to Buddhist funeral rites such as sticking chopsticks upright in rice, crossing them, passing food between them, spearing food, pointing, and rubbing splintered wabashi together.

segments.title: Using chopsticks, chopstick rests and fun facts
segments.summary: The hosts describe how to hold and move chopsticks, the etiquette for eating rice and soup, chopstick rests, serving from communal dishes, and fun facts such as the Korean marriage superstition, the uneven pair superstition, and the muscles used.

segments.title: Chopsticks, popcorn study and consecutive a phobia
segments.summary: The hosts mention a study finding that eating popcorn with chopsticks is more enjoyable, then discuss consecutive a phobia, an irrational fear of chopsticks.

segments.title: Listener mail: Sammy Davis Jr. story
segments.summary: A listener named Andrew from Pittsburgh shares a story about Sammy Davis Jr. and a local TV interview, plus a mention of his podcast Pittsburgh Oddcast.
